los.text: Describe the common causes, investigations, diagnosis and principles of treatment of an elderly patient presenting with breathing difficulty (include influenza and covid-19)
los.html:
CausesPneumonia (bacterial, influenza, COVID-19, RSV), COPD/asthma exacerbation, heart failure (pulmonary oedema), PE, AF/ACS, aspiration, anaemia, pleural effusion, sepsis with acidosis.
Atypical presentation in elderlyConfusion/delirium, falls, reduced mobility, anorexia, no fever (or hypothermia); tachypnoea is often the first sign.
AssessmentABCDE, NEWS2, sats (target 94–98%, or 88–92% if CO₂ retainer), CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP <90/≤60, age ≥65).
Ix
  • CXR
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • CRP
  • Blood cultures
  • ABG
  • ECG
  • BNP (HF)
  • D-dimer/CTPA (PE)
  • Viral PCR (nasal/throat swab: influenza A/B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV)
  • Sputum culture
  • Urinary pneumococcal/Legionella antigens if severe.
Treatment
  • Oxygen
  • Fluids
  • Antibiotics per CURB-65 (amoxicillin; + clarithromycin if moderate/severe)
  • Oseltamivir for influenza in at-risk/hospitalised patients
  • COVID-19 treatments if eligible
  • Treat HF (diuretics)
  • Bronchodilators/steroids for COPD.
  • Isolation (droplet precautions) for respiratory viruses.
HolisticEarly mobilisation, delirium prevention, hydration, nutrition, VTE prophylaxis; escalation and ceiling-of-care discussions.

los.text: Describe the impact of normal ageing in the elderly (include presentation, clinical signs and altered patterns of disease)
los.html:
Physiological changes
  • ↓ physiological reserve in every system ("homeostenosis").
  • CVS: stiffer arteries (↑ systolic BP), ↓ max HR, ↓ baroreflex sensitivity → orthostatic hypotension.
  • Resp: ↓ elastic recoil, ↓ cough reflex, ↓ immune function → pneumonia.
  • Renal: ↓ GFR (creatinine may look "normal" due to ↓ muscle mass) → drug accumulation.
  • CNS: ↓ neurons, slower processing → vulnerability to delirium.
  • MSK: sarcopenia, osteoporosis; ↓ thirst; ↓ thermoregulation; immunosenescence; ↓ vision/hearing.
  • Pharmacology: ↑ fat (↑ Vd of lipophilic drugs), ↓ hepatic and renal clearance, ↑ sensitivity (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics).
Altered presentationNon-specific "geriatric giants": falls, immobility, confusion/delirium, incontinence, iatrogenesis/polypharmacy. Silent MI, afebrile sepsis, painless abdominal catastrophes, "off legs".
Altered patternsMultimorbidity, polypharmacy (STOPP/START), atypical drug side effects, slower recovery, deconditioning in hospital.
ApproachComprehensive Geriatric Assessment (medical, functional, psychological, social, environmental) by MDT.

los.text: Explain the two main models of frailty (Phenotype and Cumulative Deficit models)
los.html:
• Frailty: state of ↑ vulnerability to stressors due to ↓ physiological reserve across multiple systems
    • minor events (UTI, new drug) cause disproportionate decline.
Phenotype model (Fried)Cumulative deficit model (Rockwood)
ConceptFrailty is a specific clinical syndromeFrailty = accumulation of health deficits
Measure5 criteria: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness (grip), slow walking speed, low physical activityFrailty Index = number of deficits present / number counted (≥30–70 items: symptoms, diseases, disabilities, test results)
Classification0 = robust; 1–2 = pre-frail; ≥3 = frailContinuous score (e.g. >0.25 frail)
ProsQuick, physical, predicts outcomesGraded, includes cognition/multimorbidity; basis of eFI in GP records
ConsIgnores cognition/psychosocialNeeds many variables
Clinical Frailty Scale (Rockwood, 1–9) used in hospitals (based on deficit model and function).
OutcomesFalls, delirium, disability, hospitalisation, care home admission, death.
ManagementCGA, exercise (resistance and balance), nutrition, medication review, falls prevention, advance care planning.

los.text: Describe the current knowledge of the pathophysiology, signs and symptoms, diagnosis and principles of treatment / management of SARS-CoV-2
los.html:
VirusSARS-CoV-2, enveloped +ssRNA betacoronavirus. Spike protein binds ACE2 (type II pneumocytes, endothelium, gut, nasal epithelium); TMPRSS2 primes entry.
Pathophysiology
  • Viral replication → (in severe disease) dysregulated immune response/cytokine storm (IL-6) → diffuse alveolar damage, ARDS
  • Endothelialitis and hypercoagulability (micro/macrothrombi, PE)
  • Multi-organ injury (myocarditis, AKI). "Silent/happy hypoxia".
SymptomsFever, cough, fatigue, myalgia, sore throat, anosmia/ageusia (earlier variants), breathlessness; GI symptoms. Long COVID: symptoms >12 weeks.
Risk of severe diseaseOlder age, immunosuppression, obesity, diabetes, CKD, unvaccinated, male sex.
DiagnosisRT-PCR (nasopharyngeal swab; gold standard), lateral flow antigen tests; bloods (lymphopenia, ↑CRP, ↑D-dimer, ↑ferritin); CXR/CT: bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities.
Management
  • Supportive
  • O₂ (target 92–96%), awake proning, CPAP/ventilation.
  • Dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days if needing O₂ (RECOVERY trial).
  • IL-6 inhibitor (tocilizumab) or baricitinib in severe disease.
  • Antivirals for high-risk non-hospitalised (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) or hospitalised (remdesivir).
  • VTE prophylaxis (LMWH).
PreventionVaccination (mRNA), isolation, ventilation, masks in healthcare.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used as anti-virals and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
DrugTarget virusMechanismKey points
Aciclovir/valaciclovirHSV, VZVGuanosine analogue; phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase → inhibits viral DNA polymerase (chain termination)IV for HSV encephalitis; nephrotoxic (crystals: hydrate), neurotoxic at high levels
Ganciclovir/valganciclovirCMVPhosphorylated by CMV UL97 kinase → DNA polymerase inhibitionMyelosuppression; teratogenic. Alternatives: foscarnet (nephrotoxic, ↓Ca/Mg), cidofovir, letermovir (prophylaxis)
Oseltamivir (oral), zanamivir (inhaled)Influenza A/BNeuraminidase inhibitors → virions can't be released from cellStart within 48 h (benefit best early; later in hospitalised/severe). Treat at-risk groups; prophylaxis in outbreaks (care homes)
Nirmatrelvir + ritonavir (Paxlovid)SARS-CoV-2Main protease (Mpro) inhibitor; ritonavir boosts levels via CYP3A4 inhibitionWithin 5 days for high-risk outpatients; many drug interactions (statins, anticoagulants, immunosuppressants)
RemdesivirSARS-CoV-2Nucleotide analogue; RNA polymerase inhibitorIV, hospitalised patients
SotrovimabSARS-CoV-2Monoclonal antibody vs spikeVariant-dependent efficacy
  • Principles: viruses use host machinery, so selective targets are limited
    • most antivirals are virustatic
    • resistance arises (TK-deficient HSV, UL97 mutations)
    • start early.

los.text: Describe virus structure and their replication strategies
los.html:
Structure
  • Nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA, single or double stranded, + or − sense) inside a protein capsid (helical or icosahedral) = nucleocapsid
  • ± lipid envelope from host membrane carrying glycoproteins (enveloped viruses are fragile, killed by detergents/alcohol; naked viruses like norovirus are hardy).
Replication cycle
  • Attachment (viral protein to host receptor: HIV gp120–CD4/CCR5; influenza haemagglutinin–sialic acid; SARS-CoV-2 spike–ACE2) → determines tropism.
  • Entry (fusion or endocytosis) → uncoating.
  • Genome replication and gene expression: DNA viruses usually in nucleus (except poxviruses); RNA viruses usually in cytoplasm (except influenza, retroviruses). +ssRNA acts directly as mRNA; −ssRNA carries its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; retroviruses use reverse transcriptase → DNA → integrate (integrase).
  • Assembly → release by budding (enveloped; acquire envelope) or lysis (naked).
Baltimore classification (I–VII) by genome type and mRNA production.
OutcomesLytic, persistent, latent (herpesviruses in neurons), transforming (HPV, EBV, HBV, HTLV-1).
RNA viruses mutate fast(no proofreading)Antigenic drift; segmented genomes (influenza) → reassortment → antigenic shift (pandemics).

los.text: Describe the interplay between viral and host factors in determining disease severity
los.html:
Viral factors
  • Virulence genes
  • Tropism (receptor distribution: e.g. avian H5N1 binds lower-airway α2,3 sialic acid → severe pneumonia)
  • Replication rate and viral load
  • Cytopathic effect
  • Immune evasion (antigenic variation, MHC downregulation, latency, interferon antagonists)
  • Inoculum dose and route
  • Toxins/superantigens.
Host factors
  • Age (very young, elderly: immunosenescence)
  • Immune status (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant, pregnancy)
  • Prior immunity (vaccination, previous infection, cross-reactivity)
  • Comorbidities (diabetes, obesity, chronic lung/heart disease)
  • Genetics (e.g. CCR5-Δ32 resists HIV; interferon pathway defects → severe COVID-19/influenza; HLA type)
  • Nutrition
  • Microbiome.
ImmunopathologyMuch tissue damage is caused by the host response (cytokine storm in COVID-19, T-cell-mediated hepatitis in HBV, dengue antibody-dependent enhancement).
Disease severityBalance between viral replication/damage and an effective but proportionate immune response.

los.text: Describe the measures to prevent and mitigate the consequences of influenza (seasonal, avian and pandemic) and covid-19 infections
sessions: MHS 1: Seasonal, avian and pandemic influenza and covid-19
los.html:
Seasonal influenza
  • Annual vaccination (antigenic drift → yearly reformulation): ≥65s
  • at-risk groups (chronic disease, immunosuppressed)
  • Pregnant women
  • Children (live attenuated intranasal LAIV age 2 to secondary school)
  • Healthcare/social care workers.
  • Antivirals for treatment/post-exposure prophylaxis in at-risk groups and care home outbreaks.
Avian influenza(H5N1, H7N9)Zoonotic; surveillance of birds/poultry workers, culling, biosecurity, PPE, antiviral prophylaxis for exposed; limited human-to-human spread.
Pandemic influenza(antigenic shift; 1918, 2009 H1N1)Pandemic preparedness plans, stockpiles of antivirals and PPE, rapid vaccine development, surveillance (WHO Global Influenza Surveillance), non-pharmaceutical interventions.
COVID-19Vaccination (booster campaigns for elderly, care home residents, immunosuppressed), testing and isolation, contact tracing, ventilation, masks, hand hygiene, antivirals for high-risk patients.
Non-pharmaceutical"Catch it, bin it, kill it", stay home when ill, isolation/cohorting in hospitals, droplet precautions (FFP3 for AGPs), social distancing/lockdowns in extremis.
MitigationSurge capacity planning, protection of vulnerable groups, communication.

los.text: Describe how the recommended immunisation schedule for children in the UK reduces morbidity and mortality for these diseases
los.html:
PrincipleHigh population coverage protects individuals and gives herd immunity (protects those who can't be vaccinated). Measles needs ~95% coverage.
UK routine childhood schedule(Green Book; updated 2025–26, so check the current version)
AgeVaccines
8 weeks6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB), MenB, rotavirus
12 weeks6-in-1, rotavirus, MenB (2nd dose moved here in 2025)
16 weeks6-in-1, PCV (pneumococcal)
1 yearMenB booster, PCV booster, MMR (MMRV from 2026)
18 months (new, 2026)6-in-1 booster, 2nd MMR(V)
3 yr 4 mo4-in-1 preschool booster (dTaP/IPV)
2–16 yrAnnual nasal flu (LAIV)
12–13 yrHPV (single dose)
14 yr3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV), MenACWY
Impact
  • Dramatic falls in Hib meningitis/epiglottitis, MenC, pneumococcal disease, rotavirus admissions, polio elimination, measles control.
  • Falls in uptake → outbreaks (measles in Wales 2013 and England 2023–24).
Contraindications
  • Live vaccines (MMR, rotavirus, LAIV, BCG) in severe immunosuppression
  • True anaphylaxis to previous dose.
  • Not contraindicated: minor illness, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), egg allergy (most).
SelectiveBCG (high TB-risk areas/families), hepatitis B at birth (HBsAg+ mothers), pertussis and RSV vaccines in pregnancy.
